Sanskrit and scripts

Sanskrit and Indian knowledge systems: a historical guide

Sanskrit is an Indo-Aryan language with a record of more than three thousand years, from the Rigveda to classical poetry, science and philosophy. Indian knowledge systems are the bodies of learning recorded in Sanskrit, Prakrit, Pali, Tamil and other languages: grammar, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, philosophy, architecture and the arts, best understood in their historical setting.

We teach India's languages and scripts historically, through lectures on linguistic heritage, Brahmi workshops and first courses in Prakrit, Pali and Śāradā, online or in person.

What is Sanskrit?

Sanskrit belongs to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European family, which also includes Persian, Greek, Latin and most European languages. The relationship was noticed by several scholars and made famous by William Jones in 1786. The name saṃskṛta means 'refined' or 'put together', in contrast to the Prakrits, the 'natural' spoken languages.

Two stages are usually distinguished. Vedic Sanskrit is the language of the Vedas, composed and transmitted orally from about the middle of the second millennium BCE. Classical Sanskrit is the standardised language described by Panini around the 5th or 4th century BCE and used for literature, science and administration for the next two thousand years. Sanskrit is one of India's classical languages and is listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.

Is Sanskrit the mother of all languages?

No. This is a common claim, but linguists agree that Sanskrit is a sister of Greek, Latin, Avestan and the other old Indo-European languages, all descended from a reconstructed ancestor called Proto-Indo-European. Sanskrit is not the source of Dravidian languages such as Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam, nor of Austroasiatic or Tibeto-Burman languages spoken in India, though all of these have borrowed Sanskrit words and Sanskrit has borrowed from them.

Sanskrit's real importance does not need exaggeration. It preserves a very old stage of Indo-European, it has an unbroken literary tradition of great size, and it was the shared learned language across South and Southeast Asia for centuries.

Scripts: how Sanskrit was written

Sanskrit has no script of its own. For most of its early life it was transmitted orally, and when it was written down it used whatever script was common in the region. The earliest deciphered Indian script is Brahmi, used in Ashoka's edicts in the 3rd century BCE, though those edicts are in Prakrit. The earliest substantial Sanskrit inscriptions come later, such as the Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman around 150 CE.

Brahmi gave rise to almost all later Indian scripts, including Gupta, Siddhamatrika, Sharada (Śāradā) in Kashmir, Grantha in the south, Bengali, Odia and Devanagari, as well as Tibetan and many scripts of Southeast Asia. Our Sanskrit alphabet explainer shows the sound order that all these scripts share, and ancient scripts of India traces the family. Talaash Heritage runs a lecture on India's scripts from Brāhmī to Śāradā and a dedicated Śāradā script course.

Panini and Sanskrit grammar

Panini's Ashtadhyayi ('eight chapters') is a grammar of about 4,000 short rules, composed around the 5th or 4th century BCE in the north-west of the subcontinent. It describes the sounds, word formation and sentence structure of Sanskrit with a precision that modern linguists still admire. The rules are ordered, use technical markers and apply in a set sequence, so that correct forms can be generated step by step.

Panini built on earlier grammarians whom he names, and his work was explained by Katyayana and Patanjali, whose Mahabhashya dates to about the 2nd century BCE. The tradition also produced phonetics (shiksha) and etymology (nirukta). Comparisons with computer languages are often made; the fair version is that Panini's system is a formal, rule-based description, and modern linguists such as Leonard Bloomfield studied it closely. Our Sanskrit grammar basics explainer gives a beginner's view.

Vedic literature

The Vedas and Upanishads are the oldest layer. There are four Vedas: Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva. Each has a core collection of hymns or formulas (samhita), followed by ritual prose texts (Brahmanas), forest texts (Aranyakas) and philosophical dialogues (Upanishads). Dates are debated, but most scholars place the Rigveda's composition around 1500 to 1200 BCE and the early Upanishads around 800 to 500 BCE.

The Vedas were preserved for centuries by oral recitation, using memory techniques that guard against change. Vedic chanting is on UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Later Vedic auxiliary sciences, the Vedangas, cover phonetics, ritual, grammar, etymology, metre and astronomy for fixing ritual times.

Classical Sanskrit literature

The two epics, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, took shape over several centuries, roughly from around 400 BCE to 400 CE. The Puranas, compiled over a long period, gather myth, genealogy and religious teaching. Classical Sanskrit literature also includes court poetry (kavya) by Ashvaghosha, Kalidasa, Bharavi, Magha and others; drama such as Kalidasa's Abhijnanashakuntalam and Shudraka's Mricchakatika; story collections such as the Panchatantra; and prose romances such as Bana's Kadambari.

Sanskrit was also the language of the Buddhist Mahayana, of Jain scholarship from the early centuries CE, and of inscriptions recording royal grants across South and Southeast Asia, from Kashmir to Cambodia.

Prakrit and Pali

Alongside Sanskrit, the spoken Middle Indo-Aryan languages, the Prakrits, were used for inscriptions, religious texts and literature. Ashoka's edicts are in Prakrit. The Jain canon is in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit. Sanskrit plays give lines to women and ordinary characters in Prakrit, and there is fine Prakrit poetry, such as Hala's Gathasaptashati. Pali is the language of the Theravada Buddhist canon, preserved in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

Prakrit and Pali are essential for early Indian history, since most inscriptions before about the 4th century CE are in Prakrit. Talaash Heritage runs introductory courses in Prakrit and Pali for students of history, Buddhism and Jainism.

Indian knowledge systems in historical context

The phrase Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS) is now used in Indian education policy for the traditions of learning developed in India. Taken historically, these traditions are substantial, and they are best presented with dates, texts and evidence rather than sweeping claims.

Historians also note what these traditions did not do. Ancient texts do not describe aircraft, nuclear weapons or modern genetics, and such claims damage the reputation of the real achievements. Knowledge also travelled both ways: Indian astronomy drew on Babylonian and Greek models, and Indian numerals passed to the Arab world and then to Europe. Scholars wrote in Tamil, Prakrit, Persian and other languages as well as Sanskrit, so IKS is wider than any one language.

Indian manuscripts

Most Indian knowledge survives in manuscripts written on palm leaf, birch bark and, from the medieval period, paper. India holds one of the largest manuscript collections in the world, in libraries, temples, monasteries, mosques, universities and family homes. The National Mission for Manuscripts, set up in 2003, has been surveying and cataloguing them. Our page on Indian manuscripts explains materials, scripts and how to visit collections.

Many manuscripts are fragile and uncatalogued, and the number of people who can read older scripts such as Sharada, Grantha or Nandinagari is small. Palaeography and preventive conservation are therefore urgent skills for anyone who wants to work with these sources.

How to start learning Sanskrit

Begin with the script and sounds. Learn Devanagari, or the script of your own language, and practise reading aloud. Then learn the noun and verb patterns slowly, with short sentences. A grammar such as M. R. Kale's Higher Sanskrit Grammar, Robert Goldman's Devavanipravesika or Michael Coulson's Teach Yourself Sanskrit gives structure; read simple texts such as the Hitopadesha alongside. Our learn Sanskrit for beginners guide sets out a realistic plan.

If your interest is historical, add a script course and some Prakrit. Reading even a short inscription in its original script is the quickest way to see how language, writing and history fit together. A good starting point is our lecture on India's linguistic heritage, followed by the Brahmi workshop.

Questions people ask

How old is Sanskrit?

The oldest form, Vedic Sanskrit, is found in the Rigveda, which most scholars date to around 1500 to 1200 BCE on linguistic grounds. Classical Sanskrit was standardised by Panini around the 5th or 4th century BCE. The oldest written Sanskrit inscriptions date from around the 1st century BCE to 2nd century CE.

Which script is used to write Sanskrit?

Sanskrit has been written in many scripts, including Brahmi, Gupta, Sharada, Grantha, Bengali, Telugu, Kannada and Devanagari. Today Devanagari is the most common, but writing Sanskrit in a regional script is entirely traditional.

Who was Panini?

Panini was a grammarian from the north-west of the subcontinent who composed the Ashtadhyayi, a grammar of about 4,000 rules, around the 5th or 4th century BCE. It is one of the earliest and most complete formal descriptions of any language.

What are Indian Knowledge Systems?

Indian Knowledge Systems is a term for the traditions of learning developed in India, including grammar, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, philosophy, architecture and the arts. They are recorded in Sanskrit, Prakrit, Pali, Tamil and other languages and are best studied with their dates and historical context.

Is Sanskrit the oldest language in the world?

No language can be called the oldest, since all spoken languages descend from earlier ones. Sanskrit is one of the oldest recorded Indo-European languages, alongside Hittite and Mycenaean Greek, which have earlier written records. Tamil also has a very long literary history.

What is the difference between Sanskrit, Prakrit and Pali?

Sanskrit is the formal, standardised language of learning. Prakrits are the Middle Indo-Aryan languages that developed from the spoken speech of the time and were used in inscriptions and Jain texts. Pali is a Middle Indo-Aryan language used for the Theravada Buddhist canon.

How long does it take to learn Sanskrit?

With regular study, most adults can read simple prose with a dictionary in about a year. Reading classical poetry or technical texts comfortably takes several years. Learning the script and basic grammar first, and reading aloud daily, speeds things up.
